title: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
summary: How GraphRAG turns a corpus into an LLM-extracted entity graph, clusters it with Leiden, pre-writes community reports, and answers whole-corpus questions by map-reduce, plus what that costs.
outcomes: Explain why top-k chunk retrieval fails on global sensemaking questions and how GraphRAG reframes them
Trace LLM entity and relationship extraction, gleaning, merging and description summarization on a toy corpus
Compute modularity for a partition and explain what Leiden's refinement phase guarantees over Louvain
Walk through map-reduce global search and choose a community level for a cost and quality target
Count indexing LLM calls and compare GraphRAG with FastGraphRAG, LightRAG and HippoRAG

lessons.title: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'

blocks.md:
In the RAG course you built the standard pipeline: split documents into chunks, embed them, retrieve the top k chunks closest to the question, and let the LLM answer from those. Edge et al. call this **vector RAG**. It works when the answer lives in a few chunks.

This course is about questions where it does not: **global questions** such as "What are the main risks facing this company?" or "What are the key themes in these podcasts?" The answer is spread across the whole corpus, and no single chunk is similar to the question.

The GraphRAG paper (Edge et al., Microsoft Research, arXiv 2404.16130) names this task **query-focused summarization (QFS)**: produce a summary of a whole corpus, shaped by a question. Classic QFS methods summarize all the text, which does not scale to the million-token corpora RAG targets. Vector RAG scales, but only ever sees k chunks.

GraphRAG combines the two: it spends LLM calls *at indexing time* to build a summarized structure of the corpus, so that a global question can be answered from those summaries instead of raw chunks.

Our running example is a corpus of 8 short chunks about a fictional startup, **Quillfern Labs**:

1. c1: Ada Moss founded Quillfern Labs and leads its Rover X2 delivery robot program.
2. c2: Every Rover X2 uses drive motors supplied by Kite Motors.
3. c3: In March a faulty Kite Motors batch triggered the Rover X2 recall.
4. c4: Ada Moss announced the recall and paused shipments from the Pune plant.
5. c5: The Pune plant assembles every Rover X2.
6. c6: Quillfern Labs closed a Series B round led by Northgate Capital.
7. c7: Quillfern CFO Ben Ortiz, formerly a Northgate Capital partner, negotiated the Series B.
8. c8: Northgate Capital also backs Corvid Drones, a rival delivery startup.

blocks.prompt: A user asks: "What are the main risks facing Quillfern Labs?" A retriever picks the top 2 chunks by similarity to the question. Which two chunks do you expect, and do they contain the risks?
blocks.reveal:
With a TF-IDF word-overlap retriever (computed by script, stop words removed), only three chunks share any term with the question, through the words *Quillfern* and *Labs*: **c6** (score 0.410, the Series B), **c1** (0.370, the founding) and c7 (0.151, Quillfern only). Every other chunk scores 0.

Neither contains a risk. The real risks are in c3 and c4 (a supplier caused a recall) and c8 (the lead investor backs a rival). Nothing in the question points at those words. A dense embedder behaves differently in detail, but the problem stays: the query describes a *kind* of content, not specific content.

blocks.title: Top-k retrieval for a global question

scenes.caption: Eight chunks, one global question: what are the main risks facing Quillfern Labs?
Scores against the question (simplified: a TF-IDF retriever stands in for embeddings). Only the chunks that name the company match at all.
Mark the chunks that actually describe a risk: c3 and c4 (recall caused by a supplier) and c8 (investor backs a rival). The top 2 contain none of them.
Raising k does not fix this at scale: at 1 million tokens, the risks could be scattered over hundreds of chunks, and the context window holds only a sample of them.

blocks.md:
The paper's other baseline is to skip retrieval and summarize *everything*: shuffle all source chunks into context-sized batches, have the LLM answer the question from each batch (map), then combine the partial answers (reduce). They call this **TS** (text summarization). It reads the whole corpus on every query, which is correct but expensive.

GraphRAG keeps the map-reduce idea but runs it over **community summaries**: compact reports about groups of related entities, written once at indexing time. The next lessons build that index step by step.

blocks.title: The GraphRAG pipeline at a glance

scenes.caption: Indexing, part 1: split the corpus and have an LLM read every chunk to extract entities and relationships. This is where most of the LLM cost goes.
Indexing, part 2: merge the per-chunk extractions into one graph, then partition it into communities of densely connected entities. This step needs no LLM.
Indexing, part 3: an LLM writes a report for every community. These reports are the index that global questions will read.
Query time: each batch of community reports produces a partial answer in parallel (map), and the best partial answers are combined into one global answer (reduce).

blocks.md: GraphRAG moves work from query time to indexing time. It pays many LLM calls up front to turn the corpus into a graph and a set of pre-written community summaries, so that global questions can be answered by reading summaries instead of sampling chunks.

GraphRAG is not a better retriever for every question. For a specific fact ("Who supplies Rover X2 motors?") plain vector RAG already finds c2, and the paper itself shows vector RAG gives the most *direct* answers. GraphRAG's measured gains are on broad sensemaking questions.

blocks.question: Which question is the best fit for GraphRAG's global search rather than plain vector RAG?
options: What year was Quillfern Labs founded?
Across all 2,000 support tickets, what recurring complaint themes appear?
Which supplier makes the Rover X2 drive motors?
What is Ben Ortiz's job title?
blocks.explain: The ticket-themes question needs a summary over the whole corpus, with no single chunk similar to the query. The other three are local fact lookups that top-k retrieval answers well and more cheaply.

blocks.question: Why does increasing k (retrieving more chunks) not solve global questions on a 1-million-token corpus?
options: Because embeddings cannot represent questions
Because LLMs cannot read more than 10 chunks
Because chunks overlap by 100 tokens
Because the retrieved set is still ranked by similarity to the question and bounded by the context window, so it is a biased sample, not the whole corpus
blocks.explain: Retrieval chooses what is similar to the question words, and the context window caps how much fits. For "main themes" the relevant evidence is everywhere, so any top-k set is a sample presented as if it were a global view.

lessons.title: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction

blocks.md:
The first indexing stage turns each chunk (GraphRAG calls it a **TextUnit**) into a small graph. An LLM reads the chunk and lists:

- **entities**: a name, a type, and a short description;
- **relationships**: a source entity, a target entity, a description of how they relate, and a numeric strength.

The entity types come from configuration. In the current microsoft/graphrag defaults they are organization, person, geo and event. Our toy adds a product type so that Rover X2 is kept.

The default prompt asks for one delimited tuple per record, which the code then parses with plain string splitting. For chunk c3 the output would look like the block below (descriptions shortened). Names are upper-cased during parsing, which is the first step of merging.

blocks.code:
("entity"<|>KITE MOTORS<|>ORGANIZATION<|>Supplier whose faulty March batch of motors triggered a recall)
##
("entity"<|>ROVER X2<|>PRODUCT<|>Delivery robot recalled after a faulty motor batch)
##
("entity"<|>RECALL<|>EVENT<|>March recall of Rover X2 robots)
##
("relationship"<|>KITE MOTORS<|>RECALL<|>Kite Motors' faulty batch caused the recall<|>8)
##
("relationship"<|>ROVER X2<|>RECALL<|>Rover X2 robots were recalled<|>9)
##
("relationship"<|>ROVER X2<|>KITE MOTORS<|>Kite Motors supplies Rover X2 motors<|>7)
<|COMPLETE|>
blocks.caption: Illustrative extraction for chunk c3 in GraphRAG's tuple format. The last field of a relationship is the LLM's strength score.

blocks.md:
**Chunk size is a cost and recall knob.** Fewer, larger chunks mean fewer LLM calls, but the paper reports that GPT-4 extracted almost twice as many entity references from 600-token chunks as from 2400-token chunks on a HotPotQA sample. The current docs default to 1200-token chunks with 100 tokens of overlap.

To recover what large chunks miss, GraphRAG uses **gleaning**, a self-reflection step: after the first extraction it tells the model that "MANY entities and relationships were missed" and asks it to add them, then optionally asks a yes or no question about whether more remain. The loop below is a simplified copy of the repo's `GraphExtractor`.

blocks.title: Counting LLM calls in the gleaning loop

scenes.caption: Default config: max_gleanings = 1. The first extraction is LLM call 1.
One continuation call asks for the missed entities and appends them. That is call 2.
With max_gleanings = 1, i = 0 is already the last round, so the loop breaks before the yes or no check. Default cost: 2 calls per chunk.
With max_gleanings = 2, round 0 does not break. The model is asked whether more entities remain (call 3) and answers Y.
Round 1 makes a second continuation call (call 4) and then breaks. Worst case for max_gleanings = g is 2g calls per chunk.

blocks.md:
**Merging.** The per-chunk subgraphs are combined. In the current code, entities with the same title and type merge into one node that keeps a *list* of descriptions; relationships with the same source and target merge into one edge whose weight is the sum of the strength scores. The paper describes the same idea with weight equal to the number of duplicate extractions, which is what our toy uses for simplicity.

**Description summarization.** A node seen in several chunks now has several descriptions. An LLM call condenses each list into one description. Elements with a single description need no call.

blocks.title: Eight chunks become one entity graph

scenes.caption: Chunk c1 yields three entities and three relationships. Each extraction is a small subgraph local to that chunk.
Chunks c2 and c3 add Kite Motors and the recall. ROVER X2 to KITE MOTORS is extracted in both chunks, so the two instances merge into one edge of weight 2.
Chunks c4 and c5 attach the Pune plant and link Ada Moss to the recall. Matching is by exact name, so every 'Rover X2' mention lands on the same node.
Chunks c6 to c8 add the funding story. The full graph has 10 nodes and 15 edges with total weight 16. Nothing in it says yet which nodes form a topic.

blocks.md: Entity matching is exact string matching (the paper says so explicitly). If one chunk says "Quillfern Labs" and another says "Quillfern", you get two nodes. The paper notes GraphRAG is fairly resilient because such duplicates usually end up in the same community, but in practice prompt tuning or an entity-resolution pass matters.

Counting our toy's description summaries: 8 of the 10 entities appear in 2 or more chunks (Rover X2 in 4; Quillfern Labs and Northgate Capital in 3; the rest except Ben Ortiz and Corvid Drones in 2), so they each need 1 summarization call. Only one relationship (Rover X2 to Kite Motors) was extracted twice, so 1 more call. That is 9 summarization calls on top of 16 extraction calls.

The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus, not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

blocks.question: A chunk is extracted with max_gleanings = 3 and the model always answers Y to the yes or no check. How many LLM calls does that chunk cost?
blocks.explain: One initial call, then 3 continuation calls, plus a yes or no check after rounds 0 and 1 (round 2 breaks before checking): 1 + 3 + 2 = 6, which is 2g for g = 3.

blocks.question: After merging, the node QUILLFERN LABS has descriptions from 3 chunks and BEN ORTIZ has one. How many description-summarization LLM calls do these two nodes need?
blocks.explain: Only lists with more than one description are sent to the LLM. QUILLFERN LABS needs 1 call; BEN ORTIZ keeps its single description as is.

lessons.title: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm

blocks.md:
A graph of thousands of entities is still too big to summarize in one prompt. GraphRAG's key move is to **partition** it into **communities**: groups of nodes with many edges inside the group and few edges leaving it. Each community becomes the unit that one LLM call summarizes.

Finding communities needs no LLM. It is classic network science, and GraphRAG uses the **Leiden** algorithm (Traag, Waltman and van Eck, 2019), applied hierarchically.

How do we score a partition? **Modularity** compares the edges that fall inside communities with the number you would expect if edges were rewired at random while keeping every node's degree. For community $c$, let $L_c$ be the (weighted) number of edges inside it, $k_c$ the sum of degrees of its nodes, and $m$ the total edge weight of the graph. The resolution $\gamma$ is usually 1.

blocks.caption: First term: the fraction of edge weight inside c. Second term: the fraction expected inside c by chance. Q is high when communities hold far more internal edges than chance predicts.

blocks.md:
Worked numbers for our toy graph (computed with networkx, weighted, $\gamma = 1$). Total weight $m = 16$ (15 edges, one with weight 2).

- Community A = {Ada Moss, Rover X2, Kite Motors, Recall, Pune plant}: $L_A = 8$, $k_A = 18$, term $= 8/16 - (18/32)^2 = 0.5 - 0.3164 = 0.1836$.
- Community B = {Quillfern Labs, Series B, Northgate Capital, Ben Ortiz, Corvid Drones}: $L_B = 6$, $k_B = 14$, term $= 6/16 - (14/32)^2 = 0.375 - 0.1914 = 0.1836$.

So $Q = 0.367$. A brute-force search over every 2-way split confirms nothing beats it, and both Leiden and Louvain return exactly this partition.

blocks.prompt: Start from that best partition and move one node to the other community. Which single move do you think hurts modularity most: moving Quillfern Labs into A, or moving Rover X2 into B?
blocks.reveal:
Moving **Rover X2** is far worse: Q drops from 0.367 to **0.094**. Rover X2 has 6 units of edge weight and 5 of them stay in A, so moving it turns most of A's internal edges into crossing edges.

Moving **Quillfern Labs** only drops Q to **0.305**, because it is a bridge with exactly two edges to each side. Bridges that connect topics are the nodes whose assignment is least certain.

blocks.title: Modularity of different partitions of the toy graph

scenes.caption: Putting all nodes in one community gives Q = 0: everything is inside, but that is also exactly what chance predicts.
Every node alone gives a negative Q (-0.115): there are no internal edges, but the chance term is still subtracted.
The product and funding split reaches Q = 0.367, the maximum over all 2-way splits.
Single-node moves from the best split: moving the bridge Quillfern costs a little (0.305); moving the hub Rover X2 wrecks the structure (0.094).
The same graph before clustering. Only 2 of the 15 edges (Ada Moss to Quillfern, Quillfern to Rover X2) will end up crossing between the two groups.
Leiden (and Louvain) on the weighted graph return two communities: product and supply (blue) and funding (orange). Modularity Q = 0.367.
Surprise: Quillfern Labs, the company itself, lands in funding. It has 2 edges to each side; the tie breaks on the chance term, since A already holds degree 18. Structure, not meaning, decides.
Each community has 5 nodes, under the default max_cluster_size of 10, so hierarchical Leiden stops here: these two are leaf communities and get one report each.

blocks.md:
**Why Leiden rather than Louvain?** Louvain, the older popular modularity optimizer, alternates two phases: move single nodes to the neighbouring community that most improves Q, then collapse each community into one node and repeat. Traag et al. showed this can produce communities that are badly connected or even internally disconnected; in their experiments up to 25% of communities were badly connected and up to 16% disconnected.

Leiden adds a **refinement** phase between moving and aggregating: inside each community it re-merges nodes starting from singletons, so only well-connected subsets are collapsed. It is proven to return connected communities, and the authors also found it faster than Louvain.

**Hierarchy.** The paper applies Leiden recursively: find communities, then detect sub-communities inside each, until leaves cannot be split further. Each level is a complete partition of the graph, labelled C0 (root, fewest communities) down to C3 in the paper's experiments. In the current microsoft/graphrag code, clustering uses `hierarchical_leiden` from graspologic-native (the Rust core of graspologic) with a `max_cluster_size` (default 10): a community larger than that is split again. Our 5-node communities are already small enough, so the toy has a single level.

Communities come from edge structure alone. Leiden never reads a description; it only sees nodes and weighted edges. That is why the extraction quality from lesson 2 decides the quality of the topics.

Modularity has a known resolution limit: on very large graphs it can merge small, genuine communities. Raising $\gamma$ yields more, smaller communities. GraphRAG's recursive splitting is another way to get fine-grained groups.

blocks.question: Community X has internal weight $L_X = 4$ and degree sum $k_X = 12$ in a graph with $m = 20$. What is its modularity term?
blocks.explain: $L_X/m = 4/20 = 0.20$ and $(k_X/2m)^2 = (12/40)^2 = 0.09$, so the term is 0.11. Dividing by $m$ rather than $2m$ in the second term is the common slip.

blocks.question: Louvain returns a community whose nodes split into two parts with no path between them inside the community. What does Leiden change to prevent this?
options: It uses a higher resolution parameter
It runs Louvain several times and averages the result
It deletes low-weight edges before clustering
It refines each community from singletons before aggregation, so only well-connected subsets are collapsed into one node
blocks.explain: The refinement phase is Leiden's core addition. Aggregating the refined partition means a community that has become disconnected can still be split apart later.

lessons.title: Community summaries and map-reduce global search

blocks.md:
Each community now gets a **community report** written by an LLM. The paper fills the prompt in priority order: for each edge in decreasing order of combined source and target degree, add the source node's description, the target node's description, the edge description and related claims, until the token limit is reached. Prominent structure goes in first.

In community A the top edge is Rover X2 to Recall (degree 5 + 4 = 9), then Ada Moss to Rover X2 (3 + 5 = 8).

For **higher-level** communities, the raw element descriptions may not fit. The paper's rule: if they fit, summarize them directly; otherwise replace sub-communities' element descriptions with their (shorter) sub-community reports, largest first, until the context fits. That is how summaries roll up the hierarchy.

The repo's report prompt asks for JSON with a title, an executive summary, an impact severity rating from 0 to 10, a one-sentence rating explanation, and 5 to 10 findings with data references.

blocks.code:
Report A  Rover X2 supply chain and recall
  summary: Quillfern's Rover X2 robot depends on a single motor supplier,
    Kite Motors. A faulty March batch triggered a recall announced by
    Ada Moss, and shipments from the Pune plant were paused.
  findings: single-supplier dependency; recall; paused production

Report B  Quillfern funding and Northgate Capital
  summary: Quillfern closed a Series B led by Northgate Capital. CFO Ben
    Ortiz, a former Northgate partner, negotiated it. Northgate also
    backs Corvid Drones, a rival delivery startup.
  findings: investor-rival overlap; CFO tied to lead investor
blocks.caption: Our two community reports, condensed and written by hand to show the shape. Real reports are longer and cite entity and relationship ids.

blocks.md:
**Global search** answers a question from the reports of one chosen hierarchy level, in map-reduce form:

1. **Prepare**: shuffle the reports and pack them into batches of a fixed token size. Shuffling spreads related material across batches so that no single context window holds (and might lose) all of it.
2. **Map**: for each batch in parallel, the LLM writes key points that answer the question, each with an **importance score from 0 to 100**. Points scored 0 are dropped.
3. **Reduce**: sort all surviving points by score, add them to one context until the token budget is full, and generate the final answer.

blocks.title: Global search over the two toy reports

scenes.caption: The question arrives. Simplified: with a toy budget of one report per batch, each report gets its own map call; real batches hold many reports.
Map calls run in parallel, one per batch. Each sees only its batch plus the question.
Each map call returns scored key points (illustrative scores). The supply-chain points score high; the CFO link is a weaker risk.
Reduce: points are sorted 85, 70, 55, 20 and packed into one context until the token budget is full (all 4 fit here), then the final answer is written.

blocks.md:
Compare this with lesson 1: chunk retrieval returned c6 and c1, with no risk in them. Global search found the supplier risk and the investor overlap because **every** community was asked, and the communities were defined by the graph rather than by similarity to the question.

The cost: one map call per batch. The paper measured how many tokens each level needs per query on its Podcast corpus (about 1 million tokens of transcripts):

blocks.title: Context tokens per global query (Podcast corpus)

scenes.caption: Source-text map-reduce (TS) reads all 1669 chunks, about 1.01 million tokens, on every query.
Low-level reports (C3) need 746,100 tokens: 26 to 33% fewer than TS across the two datasets.
Root-level reports (C0) need only 26,657 tokens, 2.6% of TS. The paper reports C0 still beat vector RAG on comprehensiveness (72% win rate).

blocks.md:
GraphRAG also offers other query modes over the same index (from the official docs):

- **Local search**: embed the question, find the most similar *entities*, then fan out to their relationships, neighbours, community reports and source text units, and fit the best of these into one context window. Suited to questions about specific entities.
- **DRIFT search**: starts like global search with the top K most relevant community reports to draft an answer and follow-up questions, then refines with local searches.
- **Basic search**: plain top-k vector RAG, for comparison.

Global search is not cheap per query. The docs call it resource-intensive: the map step makes one LLM call per batch of reports, so lower (more detailed) levels cost more calls. Picking the community level is a quality versus cost dial.

Global search never retrieves by similarity. It asks every community at one level, lets the LLM score how useful each partial answer is, and keeps the best points. That is what makes it work for questions that look like nothing in the corpus.

blocks.question: In the map step, one batch returns only points with importance score 0. What happens to them?
options: They are filtered out before the reduce step
They are kept but sorted last
They trigger a retry with a larger batch
They are replaced by raw text chunks
blocks.explain: Both the paper and the repo drop score-0 answers. If every map answer scores 0, the repo returns a canned "I do not know" unless general knowledge is explicitly allowed.

blocks.question: You need to answer 200 broad questions a day over the same corpus and cost matters most. Based on the paper's Podcast results, which level is the best starting point?
options: C3, because it is most detailed
TS, because it reads the source text
C0, because it uses about 2.6% of TS's tokens while still beating vector RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity
Vector RAG, because it is cheapest
blocks.explain: The paper recommends root-level summaries for repeated global queries: dramatically fewer tokens with a modest drop versus other global methods. Vector RAG is cheapest but loses on comprehensiveness and diversity for these questions.

lessons.title: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured

blocks.md:
Let us count LLM calls for the toy under a simplified model of the standard pipeline: default max_gleanings = 1, claim extraction off (it is off by default), one call per summarized description, one call per community report.

- Extraction: 8 chunks x 2 calls = **16**
- Entity description summaries: **8**
- Relationship description summaries: **1**
- Community reports: **2**

Total: **27 LLM calls** to index 8 short chunks. Naive vector RAG makes **0** LLM calls at indexing; it only embeds the 8 chunks. GraphRAG also embeds, by default, the 8 text units, the 10 entity descriptions and the 2 reports: 20 vectors.

blocks.title: Indexing LLM calls for the 8-chunk toy

scenes.caption: Extraction dominates: 2 calls for each of 8 chunks. The repo docs estimate graph extraction at roughly 75% of indexing cost.
Description summaries add 9 calls, one per entity or edge with more than one description.
Two community reports bring the total to 27. Naive RAG needs no LLM call to index.

blocks.md:
Query time flips the picture only partly: naive RAG makes 1 LLM call per question; toy global search made 3 (2 map, 1 reduce). At real scale, global search makes one map call per batch of reports at the chosen level.

How does indexing scale? Extraction calls grow linearly with corpus size: about $T / (s - o)$ chunks for $T$ tokens, chunk size $s$ and overlap $o$, times calls per chunk. The plot uses the docs defaults ($s = 1200$, $o = 100$) as a starting point; move the sliders.

blocks.title: Extraction calls versus corpus size (stated model)

scenes.caption: Defaults: a 1-million-token corpus is about 909 chunks and about 1,818 extraction calls, before summaries and reports. Simplified: overlap fixed at 100 tokens.
The paper's setup used 600-token chunks: about 2,000 chunks per million tokens. Smaller chunks raise recall but double the calls.
Turning gleaning off halves the calls but loses the entities the first pass missed; the paper used gleaning to make larger chunks viable.

blocks.md: Do not estimate GraphRAG cost from the number of documents alone. Cost scales with total tokens, chunk size, gleaning rounds, the number of entities and relationships that need summaries, and the number of communities. The official docs open with a warning that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources and suggest starting small.

blocks.title: Head-to-head win rates, Podcast corpus (row beats column, %)

scenes.caption: Comprehensiveness. Each cell is how often the row condition beat the column condition over 125 questions, 5 runs each. SS is vector RAG.
Read the SS column: every global method beats vector RAG, 72% (C0) to 83% (TS).
Among global methods it is close to 50%: C2 beats TS 57% of the time, C0 ties TS at 50%. The graph's win over plain map-reduce is small.
Directness (the control). Now SS wins: 65% against C0 and 60% against C1 to C3. Vector RAG gives the most focused answers, as expected.

blocks.md:
A second experiment checked the judge with a non-LLM-preference measure: extract factual claims from each answer, count them (comprehensiveness) and cluster them (diversity). All global conditions produced more claims than vector RAG (for News, about 31.6 to 34.2 per answer versus 25.2), significant at p < .05. Among the global conditions, including TS, differences were not significant.

Empowerment was mixed: the judge valued specific examples, quotes and citations, which community summaries tend to compress away.

The headline result is GraphRAG versus vector RAG on global sensemaking questions: 72 to 83% comprehensiveness win rates on Podcast. Against map-reduce over raw text, the advantage is small; the bigger win there is token cost at query time.

blocks.question: A team reports "GraphRAG wins 80% of the time" using an LLM judge on comprehensiveness only. What is the best follow-up check, following the paper's design?
options: Nothing, 80% is decisive
Switch the judge to a smaller model
Remove the questions where GraphRAG lost
Also report a control criterion like directness, and validate with a judge-independent measure such as claim counts
blocks.explain: The paper adds directness as a control (vector RAG should win it, and does) and validates comprehensiveness and diversity with claim extraction. LLM judges have biases, so a sanity check matters.

blocks.question: Your corpus doubles from 1M to 2M tokens with the same settings. Roughly what happens to extraction LLM calls?
options: They stay the same because the graph is reused
They roughly double, because extraction runs once per chunk
They grow quadratically with the number of entity pairs
They halve because chunks get larger
blocks.explain: Extraction is one prompt (plus gleaning) per chunk, so it scales linearly with the number of chunks. Summaries and reports depend on graph size, which also tends to grow.

lessons.title: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG

blocks.md:
Full GraphRAG indexing is expensive, so several lighter designs keep the graph but drop parts of the LLM work.

**FastGraphRAG** (an indexing method in the microsoft/graphrag repo) replaces LLM extraction with NLP: entities are noun phrases (NLTK or spaCy), relationships are co-occurrence in the same text unit, and there are no descriptions to summarize. The LLM is used only for community reports, written from the raw text units. The docs say it is much cheaper but noisier, and recommend it mainly when global summary questions are the goal, with smaller chunks (50 to 100 tokens) for a better co-occurrence graph.

**LightRAG** (Guo et al., arXiv 2410.05779) also extracts entities and relations with an LLM, but drops communities. At query time an LLM call extracts two kinds of keywords: **low-level** keys (specific entities) matched against entity vectors, and **high-level** keys (themes) matched against relation vectors; one-hop neighbours are then added. The authors report under 100 tokens and one API call for retrieval, versus GraphRAG reading 610 level-2 reports of about 1,000 tokens each in their legal dataset.

LightRAG also updates incrementally by taking the union of new nodes and edges. Its paper argues GraphRAG must regenerate community reports when data changes; the GraphRAG docs now also describe an incremental update mode, so check the current behaviour before relying on either claim.

blocks.caption: The personalization vector puts equal probability on each query node and zero elsewhere. Passage scores aggregate node probabilities (simplified: HippoRAG also weights query nodes by node specificity, 1 over the number of passages containing them).

blocks.title: Personalized PageRank on the toy graph

scenes.caption: Question: "What connects Ben Ortiz to the Rover X2?" Seeds are BEN ORTIZ and ROVER X2 with equal restart probability; walks continue with probability 0.5 (networkx, weighted).
The top non-seed node is Quillfern Labs (0.091): it sits between the two seeds. Series B and Northgate follow (0.069, 0.064). The bridge emerges without any LLM reasoning.

blocks.md: Summing node scores per passage ranks **c7** first (0.508: Ben Ortiz, Series B, Northgate, Quillfern) and **c1** second (0.435: Ada Moss, Quillfern, Rover X2). Together they answer the question: Ben Ortiz is CFO of Quillfern Labs, which builds the Rover X2. One PPR pass found both hops, which is how HippoRAG reports single-step retrieval comparable to or better than iterative retrieval (IRCoT) while being 10 to 20 times cheaper and 6 to 13 times faster, per its abstract.

blocks.title: Choosing a design by question type

scenes.caption: Start from the question mix your users actually ask, not from the architecture.
Local facts: vector RAG is cheapest and most direct. No graph needed.
Multi-hop entity questions: graph traversal from query entities (PPR, local search, LightRAG's keyword matching) links passages that share no words.
Global sensemaking: pre-summarized communities and map-reduce. FastGraphRAG trades graph quality for much lower indexing cost here.

blocks.md: Failure modes to watch in any LLM-built graph: missed entities in large chunks, duplicate nodes from name variants, hallucinated relationships stated with confidence, and summaries that drop the specific quotes users need. Every later stage inherits these errors, and global answers rarely show the raw evidence.

Graph RAG variants differ in where they spend LLM calls: GraphRAG spends heavily at indexing (extraction, summaries, reports) and on map calls per global query; FastGraphRAG cuts extraction; LightRAG drops communities; HippoRAG drops summaries and lets PPR do the multi-hop work.

blocks.question: Your corpus changes every hour and users mostly ask multi-hop entity questions. Which design fits best?
options: Full GraphRAG with global search at C3
TS map-reduce over all source text
A graph with incremental node and edge updates and entity-seeded retrieval, such as LightRAG or HippoRAG-style PPR
Re-run Leiden every query
blocks.explain: Frequent updates favour designs without expensive community reports to rebuild, and multi-hop entity questions are what entity-seeded graph retrieval targets. Global search over communities is aimed at whole-corpus themes.

blocks.question: In HippoRAG's PPR step, why does Quillfern Labs score high for the question about Ben Ortiz and Rover X2, even though the question never mentions it?
options: Because random walks restarting at both seeds pass through it, so it collects probability from both sides
Because it has the longest description
Because the LLM ranked it first
Because it is in the largest community
blocks.explain: PPR mass flows outward from the seed nodes. A node adjacent to both seeds receives probability from each, which is how the bridge in a multi-hop chain surfaces without an extra retrieval round.

blocks.question: FastGraphRAG builds relationships from co-occurrence instead of LLM extraction. What do you lose?
options: Community detection, which then cannot run
Relationship and entity descriptions; edges only say that two noun phrases appeared in the same text unit, so the graph is noisier
The ability to answer global questions at all
All embeddings
blocks.explain: The docs say FastGraphRAG has no entity or relationship descriptions and a noisier graph. Leiden and community reports still run, which is why it remains useful for global summary questions.
